Example of Linear Regression(Supervised Learning)

Lifting Torque Calculation: Robot Arm

Problem Statement: Calculate how much torque is required
by a robot arm (joint-motor) to lift a box; based on the
weight of the box and how far the arm is extended?


Data Architecture
   ➢Input Features (X): Weight (kg), Extended Distance (m)
   ➢Target output (y): Torque (floating-point number)


 Algorithm: Linear Regression




                                                                                                           4

visualInspection.notes: Robot-arm photograph lifting a box has no numerical geometry labels. Problem uses Weight (kg) and Extended Distance (m) as features, torque as floating-point output, linear regression. Kilograms describe mass, and additive regression is not a general m g r law.

slides.title: Supervised Learning: Generalization
slides.text:
Supervised Learning: Generalization
•   In supervised learning, the ultimate goal is to build a model that can perform
   well on new, never-before-seen data.
➢Generalization:
A model is said to generalize if it can take the mappings learned from a training set
and apply them accurately to a test set or real-world data with similar
characteristics.
•  Model can always "memorize" a training set perfectly, the only true measure of
   generalization is its performance on a separate test set.

➢We want to build a model that is able to generalize as
   accurately as possible.




                                                                                                           8

visualInspection.notes: Accurate new data with similar characteristics; separate test set. Literal claim model can always memorize training perfectly is false for restricted model families; counterexample available in preceding affine regression.

Supervised Learning: Overfitting v/s Underfitting

              Overfitting                              Underfitting
•   It occurs when a model is too complex      •   It occurs when a model is too simple to
   relative to the amount of information         capture the essential variability and
   (training data) available.                     patterns in the data.
• When model is fit too closely to the         •  Symptoms: both training error and test
   particularities of the training set.              error HIGH.
•  Result: works well on the training set      Causes: Insufficient features; Strong
   but is not able to generalize to new data   regularization that "stifles" the model’s
•  Symptoms: LOW training error; HIGH        ability to learn.
   test error.
Causes: too many features relative to the
number of samples; too many training
iterations; Using highly flexible models.

Causes excessive feature/sample ratio, iterations, flexibility versus insufficient features and excessive regularization. Iteration statement needs algorithm/context qualification.

slides.title: Supervised Learning: Trade-off
slides.text:
Supervised Learning: Trade-off                  Trade-off of model complexity
                                                              against training and test accuracy •  Every model design decision:
                                       optimal model   ➢Number of features ,
    ➢Regularization strength,
    ➢Dataset size,
    ➢Evaluation strategy
 •  Ultimately comes down to managing the trade-
    off between underfitting and overfitting.

   Concept     Training Error   Test Error

Generalization  Low         Low       Desired Model

Overfitting     Very low       High      Model too complex

Underfitting    High           High      Model too simple



                                                                                                           10

visualInspection.notes: Accuracy versus model complexity graph has rising training curve and peaked then declining generalization curve. Sweet spot at generalization peak; underfit left, overfit right. Four design choices feature count, regularization, data size, evaluation strategy. Table low/low desired, verylow/high overfit, high/high underfit. Qualitative, not universal curve law.

slides.title: Reinforcement Learning
slides.text:
Reinforcement Learning

Machine learning framework where a decision-making agent learns to solve
problems through trial-and-error interaction with an environment.
•   Unlike supervised learning, which relies on a teacher providing correct answers,
   reinforcement learning is "learning with a critic" that provides rewards or penalties only
    after a sequence of actions is taken.
Core Elements of Reinforcement Learning
➢Agent: is the learner/decision-maker.
➢Environment: is everything outside(physical world) the agent it interacts with.
➢State (s): is representation of the current situation.
➢Action (a): a set of possible moves available to the agent
    in a given state.
The agent's goal is to maximize the cumulative reward over time.



                                                                                                          19

visualInspection.notes: Trial/error agent environment interaction; critic rewards/penalties; maximize cumulative reward. Agent learner/decision maker, environment outside agent, state current representation, action incorrectly defined as set of possible moves (action space). Only after a sequence overstates reward timing; environment need not be physical. These qualifications require explicit conflict binding when tested.

slides.title: Reinforcement Learning
slides.text:
Reinforcement Learning
The RL Learning Loop:
   ➢Robot observes STATE
   ➢Takes ACTION
   ➢Environment gives REWARD
   ➢Robot updates its Brain
   ➢Loop repeats!
Key Challenges:
➢A primary challenge in RL is the Credit Assignment.
➢Agents must learn balance Exploration vs Exploitation.
Major Algorithms:            Application:
➢Q-Learning                    ➢Autonomous Navigation
➢Sarsa                       ➢Avoiding Obstacles
➢Model-Based Learning

                                                                                                          20

visualInspection.notes: Loop observes STATE, takes ACTION, environment REWARD, updates brain, repeats; cartoon shows same clockwise sequence. Challenges credit assignment and exploration/exploitation. Named algorithms Q-Learning, Sarsa, Model-Based Learning; applications autonomous navigation and obstacle avoidance. No update equations supplied.

slides.title: Summary
slides.text:
Summary

•   It is essential in robotics wherever sensor data is too complex for hand-crafted
    rules.
•  The three major paradigms supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement
   learning each suit different robotics tasks and data availability scenarios.
•  Note: “many people spend a lot of time building complex
   machine learning solutions, only to find out they don't
   solve the right problem”





                                                                                                          21

visualInspection.notes: Recap says ML useful when sensor complexity defeats handcrafted rules; paradigms depend on tasks and available data. Unique warning: complex ML can solve the wrong problem, so retain as examinable problem-framing concept rather than blanket recap exclusion.
